excerpt: How long you have to file a personal injury lawsuit in South Carolina, and the exceptions that shorten or extend that window.
keyTakeaways: South Carolina gives personal injury victims 3 years from the date of injury to file a lawsuit (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Exceptions include: 2-year deadline for claims against government entities under the SC Tort Claims Act, tolling for minors (deadline paused until age 18), and the discovery rule (clock starts when the injury is or should have been discovered). Waiting to file weakens cases — evidence degrades, witnesses forget, and defendants destroy records.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a personal injury lawsuit in South Carolina?
faqs.answer: Three years from the date of your injury under S.C. Code § 15-3-530. It applies to car accidents, truck and motorcycle crashes, pedestrian and bicycle claims, slip and falls, dog bites and other negligence-based claims.

faqs.question: What happens if I miss the deadline?
faqs.answer: Your claim is permanently barred, no matter how serious your injuries or how clear the other driver's fault was. A court does not weigh the merits of a claim filed out of time, so the deadline is effectively absolute.

faqs.question: Is the deadline shorter for a claim against a government entity?
faqs.answer: Yes. Under the South Carolina Tort Claims Act the action is barred unless it is commenced within two years of the date the loss was or should have been discovered (S.C. Code § 15-78-110), rather than the usual three.

faqs.question: Do I have to file a notice before suing a government entity?
faqs.answer: No. There is no pre-suit notice a claimant must serve under the Tort Claims Act. Filing a verified claim with the entity is optional (S.C. Code § 15-78-80), and doing so within one year extends the deadline to three years.

faqs.question: Why does waiting hurt my case even inside the deadline?
faqs.answer: Because the proof degrades. Physical evidence disappears, witnesses forget details, and insurers notice a delayed claim and treat it as weaker. The strength of a case is usually set long before the filing deadline arrives.
